site.title: Important papers.
site.lead: Landmark critical care, trauma and perioperative papers, rounded up by Kenji Tanabe. Each card has the takeaway, why it matters, the Wiki Journal Club summary where there is one, and a link to the full paper.

pages.title: SAFE: Albumin vs Saline
pages.blurb: 6,997 ICU patients got 4% albumin or normal saline for resuscitation. 28-day mortality was the same (RR 0.99), as were organ failure, ICU days and ventilator days.
pages.why: Showed colloid and crystalloid are roughly equivalent for the general ICU patient, so albumin became a cost and context decision. Its subgroups (a harm signal in traumatic brain injury, a possible benefit in severe sepsis) launched the next generation of trials.
tags: A Comparison of Albumin and Saline for Fluid Resuscitation in the ICU

pages.title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021
pages.source: Crit Care Med / Intensive Care Med 2021
pages.blurb: The international sepsis guideline: antibiotics within an hour for probable septic shock, balanced crystalloids, norepinephrine first with a MAP target of 65, vasopressin as a second agent, hydrocortisone for ongoing vasopressor need, and no qSOFA alone for screening.
pages.why: It is the reference most hospital sepsis bundles, order sets and quality metrics are built on, so it frames what everyone else in the room expects you to do.

pages.title: SEPSISPAM: MAP 80–85 vs 65–70
pages.blurb: 776 patients in septic shock were resuscitated to a MAP of 80–85 or 65–70. Mortality at 28 and 90 days was no different, and the high target caused more new atrial fibrillation.
pages.why: The evidence behind MAP 65 as the default target. A chronic-hypertension subgroup needed less dialysis at the higher target, which keeps individualized targets in the conversation.
tags: High versus Low Blood-Pressure Target in Patients with Septic Shock

pages.title: ARDSNet (ARMA): 6 vs 12 mL/kg
pages.blurb: 861 patients with ALI/ARDS were ventilated at 6 mL/kg predicted body weight with plateau pressure ≤30, or 12 mL/kg. Low tidal volumes cut mortality from 39.8% to 31.0% and added ventilator-free days.
pages.why: The foundation of lung-protective ventilation: tidal volume by predicted body weight and a plateau-pressure ceiling, in the ICU and increasingly in the OR.
tags: Ventilation with Lower Tidal Volumes as Compared with Traditional Tidal Volumes for ALI and ARDS

pages.title: PROSEVA: Prone Positioning
pages.blurb: 466 patients with severe ARDS (P/F <150 on FiO₂ ≥0.6) had prone sessions of at least 16 hours or stayed supine. 28-day mortality fell from 32.8% to 16.0%.
pages.why: Made early, prolonged proning standard care for moderate to severe ARDS. The details matter: started early, long sessions, in centers experienced at turning.
tags: Prone Positioning in Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome

pages.title: EOLIA: Early VV-ECMO
pages.blurb: 249 patients with very severe ARDS got immediate venovenous ECMO or conventional care with rescue ECMO allowed. 60-day mortality was 35% vs 46% (P=0.09); 28% of controls crossed over to ECMO.
pages.why: Technically negative, but the crossover and later reanalyses point toward benefit. It positioned VV-ECMO as rescue for very severe ARDS in experienced centers rather than routine early therapy.
tags: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Severe ARDS

pages.title: NICE-SUGAR: Glucose Targets
pages.blurb: 6,104 ICU adults were targeted to glucose 81–108 mg/dL or ≤180 mg/dL. Intensive control increased 90-day mortality and caused far more severe hypoglycemia.
pages.why: Ended the era of tight glucose control in the ICU. A target of roughly 140–180 mg/dL is the standard it set.
tags: Intensive versus Conventional Glucose Control in Critically Ill Patients

pages.title: MENDS2: Dexmedetomidine vs Propofol
pages.blurb: 422 ventilated adults with sepsis under light sedation got dexmedetomidine or propofol. Days alive without delirium or coma, ventilator-free days, 90-day mortality and 6-month cognition were all the same.
pages.why: Either drug is reasonable for light sedation; choose on hemodynamics, cost and the patient in front of you. The bigger lever is keeping sedation light, not which agent you use.
tags: Dexmedetomidine or Propofol for Sedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adults with Sepsis

pages.title: PROPPR: 1:1:1 vs 1:1:2
pages.blurb: 680 severely injured trauma patients predicted to need massive transfusion got plasma, platelets and red cells at 1:1:1 or 1:1:2. Overall 24-hour and 30-day mortality did not differ, but 1:1:1 achieved hemostasis more often and had fewer early deaths from exsanguination.
pages.why: The basis for balanced, ratio-driven massive transfusion protocols, and a reason to have plasma and platelets ready early rather than catching up later.
tags: Transfusion of Plasma, Platelets, and RBCs in a 1:1:1 vs 1:1:2 Ratio (PROPPR)

pages.title: TRICC: Transfuse at Hb 7 vs 10
pages.blurb: 838 euvolemic ICU patients were transfused at hemoglobin below 7 or below 10 g/dL. The restrictive strategy was at least as safe (30-day mortality 18.7% vs 23.3%) and did better in younger, less sick patients.
pages.why: Made a hemoglobin trigger of 7 the ICU default and halved transfusions. The exception it flagged, acute coronary syndromes, is still debated.
tags: A Multicenter, Randomized, Controlled Trial of Transfusion Requirements in Critical Care

pages.title: ECLS-SHOCK: VA-ECMO in AMI Shock
pages.blurb: 420 patients with infarct-related cardiogenic shock and planned early revascularization got early VA-ECMO or medical therapy alone. 30-day mortality was no lower with ECMO, and bleeding and vascular complications were higher.
pages.why: Routine early VA-ECMO for AMI shock doesn't save lives. Mechanical support needs careful patient selection, not reflex escalation.
tags: Extracorporeal Life Support in Infarct-Related Cardiogenic Shock

pages.title: PONV: 5th Consensus Guidelines
pages.blurb: The international consensus on preventing and treating postoperative nausea and vomiting. Every adult at any risk gets at least two prophylactic agents, the risk score decides how far past two to go, and rescue uses a different drug class than prophylaxis.
pages.why: Replaces risk-scaled prophylaxis, which was poorly followed and kept missing high-risk patients, with a simpler default that is easier to apply on every case.
tags: Fifth Consensus Guidelines for the Management of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting

pages.title: CRASH-2: Tranexamic Acid in Trauma
pages.blurb: 20,211 bleeding or at-risk trauma patients in 40 countries got TXA (1 g load, then 1 g over 8 h) or placebo within 8 hours of injury. TXA lowered all-cause death (14.5% vs 16.0%) and death from bleeding, without more clots.
pages.why: The reason early TXA is part of every major trauma protocol. Later analyses showed the benefit depends on giving it early, within about 3 hours of injury.

pages.title: PAMPer: Prehospital Plasma by Air
pages.blurb: 501 trauma patients at risk of hemorrhagic shock got thawed plasma or standard care during air medical transport. 30-day mortality fell from 33.0% to 23.2%, with no rise in lung injury or transfusion reactions.
pages.why: The strongest evidence that starting plasma before arrival saves lives when transport is long. Read it alongside COMBAT.

pages.title: COMBAT: Prehospital Plasma by Ground
pages.blurb: Run by Denver Health paramedics: 144 patients in hemorrhagic shock got 2 units of plasma or saline during short urban ground transport (median 16–19 minutes). No survival benefit (28-day mortality 15% vs 10%), and the trial stopped for futility.
pages.why: Our own city's trial. With PAMPer it shows context matters: prehospital plasma helps on long transports but adds little when a level 1 center is minutes away.

pages.title: TRICS-III: Transfusion in Cardiac Surgery
pages.blurb: 5,243 moderate- to high-risk cardiac surgery patients were transfused below a hemoglobin of 7.5 or a liberal threshold (below 9.5 in the OR and ICU). The restrictive strategy was noninferior for death, MI, stroke or dialysis-requiring renal failure, and fewer patients were transfused (52% vs 73%).
pages.why: Extended restrictive transfusion into the OR for a high-risk group, starting from induction. 7.5 is the cardiac-surgery threshold that guidelines now cite.

pages.title: TRISS: Transfusion in Septic Shock
pages.blurb: 998 ICU patients with septic shock were transfused at a hemoglobin of 7 or 9. 90-day mortality was the same (43% vs 45%), and the lower threshold used about half the blood.
pages.why: Settled that septic shock does not need a higher trigger, overturning the old early goal-directed habit of transfusing toward a hematocrit of 30.

pages.title: FOCUS: Transfusion After Hip Fracture
pages.blurb: 2,016 hip-fracture patients aged 50 or older with cardiovascular disease or risk factors were transfused at a hemoglobin of 10 or for symptoms (or below 8). Death or inability to walk at 60 days was the same, as were in-hospital coronary events.
pages.why: Showed restrictive transfusion is safe even in older patients with heart disease after surgery. It is the basis for the 8 g/dL threshold in orthopedic and cardiac-risk patients.

pages.title: MINT: Transfusion in Acute MI
pages.blurb: 3,504 patients with acute MI and hemoglobin below 10 were transfused at 7–8 or below 10. MI or death at 30 days was 16.9% restrictive vs 14.5% liberal (P=0.07): not significant, but leaning toward liberal.
pages.why: The exception to transfusing at 7. Harm from a restrictive strategy in acute MI could not be excluded, so many clinicians now aim for about 10 in active coronary ischemia.

pages.title: TRAIN: Transfusion in Acute Brain Injury
pages.blurb: 850 patients with TBI, subarachnoid or intracerebral hemorrhage and hemoglobin below 9 were transfused below 9 or below 7. Liberal transfusion lowered unfavorable neurologic outcome at 6 months (62.6% vs 72.6%) and cerebral ischemic events.
pages.why: The first large trial to show benefit from a higher trigger in brain injury, where the brain may not tolerate anemia. Read it alongside HEMOTION.

pages.title: HEMOTION: Transfusion in TBI
pages.blurb: 742 patients with moderate or severe TBI and anemia were transfused at 10 or 7. Unfavorable 6-month outcome was 68.4% liberal vs 73.5% restrictive, a difference that was not statistically significant; survivors did better on some function and quality-of-life scales.
pages.why: With TRAIN, it points the same direction: in brain injury a liberal trigger is reasonable and possibly better, even though HEMOTION alone was not conclusive.

pages.title: UK-REBOA: The Randomized Trial
pages.blurb: 90 patients with exsanguinating hemorrhage at 16 UK major trauma centers got ED REBOA plus standard care or standard care alone. 90-day mortality was 54% with REBOA vs 42% without (86.9% probability of harm), with more early deaths from bleeding.
pages.why: The only randomized trial of REBOA so far, and it found no benefit and probable harm when used in the ED. A strong argument for tight selection criteria and a fast path to definitive hemorrhage control.

pages.title: REBOA in US Civilian Trauma (TQIP)
pages.blurb: A propensity-matched national registry study: 140 REBOA patients vs 280 similar patients without. Mortality was higher with REBOA (35.7% vs 18.9%), as were acute kidney injury and lower-limb amputation, with no difference in blood use.
pages.why: Observational, so open to confounding, but it was the first large US warning sign and it lines up with UK-REBOA. Know the complications before the balloon goes up.

pages.title: REBOA: The First Civilian Series
pages.blurb: Six trauma patients in end-stage hemorrhagic shock at two US centers had REBOA placed by trauma surgeons (Zone I or III), raising systolic pressure by a mean of 55 mm Hg with no REBOA-related complications.
pages.why: The case series that brought REBOA into civilian trauma care and defined the zones and workflow still in use. Useful context for how the later, less favorable data came about.
